- **Regulative vs. normative principle:** concedes the terms are imprecise; argues Anglicans actually hold a *more consistent* regulative principle and that populist RPW adherents are inconsistent — incense (Exod 30; Mal 1:11; Rev 8), vestments (Exod 28; Rev 4), hymns beyond psalms (Matt 26:30; Eph 5:19), instruments (Ps 150), plus Jesus at Hanukkah and synagogue worship (neither OT-prescribed). On incense he concedes it "symbolizes the prayers" but defends the object: "a symbol doesn't work well if it's not there." **[Stated, AW-I, Recon-Euch]**  
- **[Analysis]** He refutes the *populist* RPW, not the confessional one. WCF 21.1 runs on command + approved example + good-and-necessary consequence; WCF 1.6 distinguishes **elements** (need warrant) from **circumstances** (time/place/posture, ordered by prudence). His examples tend to conflate the two or skip new-covenant fulfillment (Heb 7–10; Col 2:16–17). Incense arguably proves too much (Revelation's heavenly liturgy also has a literal altar, slain Lamb, sea of glass) — but the *external* "proves too much" point is now superseded by the *internal* levers below, which the Revelation class makes far stronger. Synagogue/Hanukkah are descriptive; the synagogue is itself a *circumstance*, illustrating rather than refuting the distinction.
- 🎯 **Incense, 2025 Mass-teaching (RC-3), pre-answers two levers at once.** (1) **Symbol-needs-presence move (★★, RC3-8):** pre-answers the Rev 5:8 "it's only a symbol of prayer" lever before it's even raised. He CONCEDES incense symbolizes prayer, then argues "a symbol doesn't work well if it's not there," so the symbolism itself is made to justify the physical incense. Confirms the strategic need to fight on the shadow-vs-substance / abrogation axis (signification, in Q1's terms), not on the symbolic axis alone, since he has an answer ready for the symbolic challenge. (2) **Burden inversion (★, RC3-9):** incense is in the OT, "never negated," present in heaven's worship, and prophesied in Malachi, so "I need a strong argument" to exclude it; answers the silence-in-Acts objection by analogy to women receiving communion. This is the operative normative-principle engine running directly against the RPW (cf. IP-2), and it is the exact mirror image of his own burden-of-proof rule on the papacy (§3, RC5-6), where the burden runs the *other* way. See QC-f in the question list; this asymmetry is the highest-value new lever in the whole incense cluster. (3) **Development confirmed (RC3-10):** Malachi 1:11 was "the final nail in the coffin" / decisive for him in 2025, and he was "not so insistent" on it when first ordained (circa 2020); by 2026 (IP-3) the warrant reweights to heaven-earth-participation-lead with Malachi as one supporting prong among others. (4) Incense is "a symbol … nothing magical about it," i.e. non-propitiatory (RC3-11), connecting to the Malachi pure-offering reserve under Q1. **[Stated, RC3-8, RC3-9, RC3-10, RC3-11]**  
- 🎯 **STRONGEST NEW INTERNAL LEVER (COT-6 vs. AW-I) — his own fulfillment hermeneutic cuts against his incense argument.** In the Christ-in-the-OT class, RJ argues *at length* that reviving OT ceremonial is wrong precisely because those rites *pointed forward* to a Christ who had not yet come, and are now *fulfilled*: "the epistle to the Hebrews warns against going back to the ways of the old covenant… now its purpose is fulfilled." He says our liturgy must point to the *present, risen* Christ, and that re-adopting uniquely-OT practices amounts to "implicitly, liturgically, ceremonially saying that this [Christ's coming] has not yet happened." **[Stated, COT-3, COT-6]**  
  - **This is the Reformed fulfillment argument against incense, in his own mouth.** His Worship-series defense of incense leans on Malachi 1:11 and the Revelation/heavenly-temple imagery — i.e., on OT-and-apocalyptic *ceremonial* warrant. But by his own COT principle, OT incense (Exod 30; the altar of incense in the Tabernacle, which he treats typologically as pointing to "the prayers of the saints" and ultimately to Christ) is a *shadow fulfilled in Christ* — so reviving it as literal gathered-worship practice is exactly the move he condemns. He even explicitly typologizes the tabernacle incense as fulfilled. The friendly question writes itself: *"You taught that Hebrews forbids reviving fulfilled OT ceremonial because it implies Christ hasn't come — how is burning literal incense, an OT tabernacle rite you yourself read as a fulfilled type, not subject to your own rule?"* This is far stronger than the external "incense proves too much" critique because it's **his own stated hermeneutic turned on his own practice** — an internal-consistency question, not a cross-tradition one.  
- 🎯🎯 **THE REVELATION CLASS NAILS THE HINGE — and complicates it (Rev-9, Rev-10, Rev-11; full detail in §18).** The 2025 Revelation class moves the incense/altar warrant from *inference* to *flat, repeated, in-his-own-voice statement*. On the golden censer and altar of Rev 8:3–5 he says: *"not only is incense being used, but an altar as well. **Again, we take a lot of our worship theology from the book of Revelation. This is one of the reasons we have incense. This is one of the reasons why we have an altar.**"* Then, stacking Exod 30 + Luke 1 + Malachi 1:11: *"a central aspect of worship, both the incense and the altar. **And that's how it is for us. We have both as part of our worship, as the standard part of our worship.**"* On the Rev 5:8 bowls of incense: *"Psalm 141:2… we see that all throughout the Old Testament, **which is why we use incense at church.**"* So the practice's stated rationale is now explicit and threefold: (a) OT prescription (Exod 30), (b) OT prophecy of NT incense (Mal 1:11), and (c) the heavenly liturgy of Revelation. This **reinforces** OQ8 decisively on the OT-revival horn — (a) and (b) are precisely the fulfilled shadows his COT hermeneutic says we must not revive.  
  - **But the Revelation class also hands him his escape hatch, and you need to see it clearly before pressing.** Threaded through the class is a *governing principle* he states outright: **earthly worship participates in / patterns itself on heavenly worship.** On the Sanctus of Rev 4:8 → the Sursum Corda: *"we are joining in the heavenly worship with the angels and archangels… we get that from Revelation 4."* On Rev 5: *"this isn't reflecting our worship. **Our worship is reflecting their worship.**"* On Rev 7: *"our worldview should be first and foremost informed by our worship."* Call this the **heavenly-pattern-participation** warrant. It is *not* the OT-revival argument, and it is not obviously subject to the COT fulfillment rule, because the worship of Rev 4–5 is presented as the *present, ongoing, post-ascension* reality of heaven — not a fulfilled-and-retired OT shadow. So if you press only the COT-vs-incense lever, he will answer: *"I'm not reviving Exodus 30; I'm joining the worship of heaven that John saw, which is happening now."* That answer neutralizes the simplest form of the question.  
  - **The sharpened question (what OQ8 now has to do).** The lever still holds, but it has to be aimed at the *seam between his two warrants*, not just the OT one. Three moves, in ascending order of force:  
    1. **The signification problem.** RJ himself says the heavenly incense *is* a symbol — Rev 5:8 and 8:3–4 *interpret* the bowls/smoke as "the prayers of the saints," and he affirms "incense is all throughout scripture symbolic of prayer." So Revelation gives him the *thing signified* (the prayers of the saints ascending) and the *interpretation of the symbol* — it does not obviously command the *physical signifier* (literal burning incense) in the earthly assembly. The heavenly altar in Rev 8 has no human celebrant lighting a thurible; the censer is in an angel's (or Christ's) hand. By what warrant does "heaven displays the reality that prayer ascends like incense" license "therefore we burn the physical substance"? This is the cleanest pressure point and it is *internal*: he reads the bowls symbolically, then materializes the symbol.  
    2. **The apocalyptic-genre problem (uses his own hermeneutic again).** He insists, correctly and repeatedly, that Revelation's imagery is *not* "woodenly literal" — the sea of glass, the slain Lamb with seven horns and seven eyes, the 24 elders, the living creatures, the bowls, the golden altar are all symbolic/typological, read through their scriptural interpretation. He will not build a literal sea of glass or seat 24 literal elders. So *why is the incense the one element of the heavenly furniture that gets reproduced as a literal physical object on earth,* when every other item in the same vision he treats as symbol pointing to a reality? The selectivity is the tension: a consistent application of his own anti-literalist apocalyptic hermeneutic would read the heavenly incense as it reads the heavenly sea — as a symbol of a reality (prayer, peace) the church *has in Christ*, not as a blueprint for sanctuary furniture.  
    3. **The fulfillment problem, restated to survive the escape hatch.** Even granting heavenly-pattern participation, his COT rule was about *which* OT shadows are fulfilled-and-retired. He typologizes the tabernacle altar of incense as a shadow of "the prayers of the saints" and ultimately of Christ's intercession (Heb 7–10; cf. §17, where Christ "daily presents himself before the Father interceding"). Revelation 8 *confirms* that typology — the heavenly reality is intercession/prayer, mediated by the angel-priest who is plausibly Christ (RJ's own read). So the heavenly scene, on his interpretation, points to *Christ's heavenly intercession and the saints' prayers* — exactly the fulfilled reality Hebrews says replaces the shadow. Reviving the *shadow's physical apparatus* (altar + incense) in the earthly assembly, when the vision itself directs us to the *fulfilled reality*, is the move his Hebrews argument forbids — now with Revelation as a witness *for* the fulfillment reading rather than against it.  
  - **[Analysis — for JD]** "Heavenly-pattern participation" is a real and respectable category, and it is *not* uniquely Eastern Orthodox, though the EO press it hardest (the Divine Liturgy as participation in the heavenly liturgy; the iconostasis as the heaven-earth boundary). It also has Roman, Lutheran, and high-Anglican forms, and there is a *thin* version even the Reformed grant. **How the classically Reformed tradition handles it** (so you can engage it without either conceding it or attacking a legitimate idea):  
    - *The Reformed do affirm a real participation.* Calvin's eucharistic doctrine is built on *sursum corda* — by the Spirit the worshipper is *lifted up to heaven* to feed on the ascended Christ, rather than Christ being brought down to the elements (*Institutes* 4.17.31–36). WCF 21 and the Heidelberg Catechism assume the gathered church joins the worship of the church triumphant. Hebrews 12:22–24 ("you have come to Mount Zion… to the assembly of the firstborn… to innumerable angels") is the Reformed proof-text that earthly worship *already* participates in the heavenly. So the Reformed answer to RJ is **not** "there is no heavenly participation" — that would be conceding the field on a point Scripture teaches. The disagreement is about **what participation licenses.**  
    - *The Reformed limit is the same one that governs the whole RPW: participation transmits the heavenly* ***realities*** *(access to God, communion with Christ and the saints, the prayers ascending, the "holy holy holy"), not a mandate to* ***reproduce the heavenly furniture as physical objects.*** The Reformed read Hebrews as teaching that the *true* tabernacle is heaven itself (Heb 8:1–5, 9:11–24) and that the earthly copies were shadows now fulfilled — so the direction of fulfillment runs *away from* re-materializing altars and incense, not *toward* it. To participate in the heavenly worship is to do by faith and the Spirit what heaven does in reality; it is *not* to build a scale model of heaven's sanctuary. The Sanctus is the test case the Reformed happily accept: we *sing* the "holy, holy, holy" with the angels (a reality-participation in the praise) — we do not therefore install a literal sea of glass, six-winged creatures, or 24 thrones. Incense is the item where RJ crosses from participating-in-the-reality to reproducing-the-furniture, and that crossing is exactly what the genre (symbol, not blueprint) and the fulfillment hermeneutic (shadow→reality, not reality→new-shadow) both forbid.  
    - *The element/circumstance distinction does the same work from the other side.* Even if heaven "uses incense," heaven's worship is not the *regulative authority* for the elements of new-covenant gathered worship — Christ's institution and apostolic practice are (WCF 21.1). The NT descriptions of gathered worship (Acts 2:42; 1 Cor 11–14; Col 3:16; Eph 5:19; 1 Tim 2) prescribe Word, prayer, sacrament, psalmody — and contain *no* instituted incense, altar-sacrifice, or thurifer for the assembly. A vision of heaven is not a church order. (This is the point where his "Jesus at the synagogue / Hanukkah" examples also fail: descriptive, not prescriptive; and the synagogue is itself a circumstance.)  
    - **Net for the conversation:** don't deny heavenly-pattern participation — affirm it warmly (Heb 12:22–24; Calvin's *sursum corda*), then locate the disagreement precisely: *participation in the heavenly reality is granted; the question is whether the vision of heaven's symbolic furniture is a* ***prescription to reproduce that furniture physically*** *in the earthly assembly — and on your own apocalyptic hermeneutic (symbol, not camcorder) and your own Hebrews/COT fulfillment hermeneutic (shadow→fulfilled reality), it isn't.* That keeps you from attacking something legitimate while still landing the internal-consistency point. This is the single strongest line in the corpus and the Revelation class both sharpened it and told you exactly which counter he'll reach for.  
    - **Sources to pull from [Analysis, added v0.8]:** the keystone is **John Owen, *An Exposition of the Epistle to the Hebrews* (chs. 8–10)** — the new-covenant priest, sacrifice, tabernacle, and altar are all *heavenly* (Christ's), and the heavenly realities could not be introduced without the *removal* of the earthly types: the precise answer to "heaven has an altar, so we have one." Pair with **Calvin, *Institutes* 4.17.31–36** (the *sursum corda*) + **Heb 12:22–24** for the participation granted, and **Calvin on Col 2:16–17** for the shadow→substance direction; codified in **WCF 21.1** and the **Westminster Directory (1645)**. The closest *historical* precedent is **intra-Anglican**: the Laudian "altar wars" of the 1630s, where the avant-garde (Andrewes, Cosin, Laud) reproduced heaven's throne-room in the chancel — at Durham, Cosin's gilded star-painted ceiling and ranks of carved angels — on a "beauty of holiness / gateway to heaven" rationale, and conforming Reformed Anglicans objected (**Peter Smart**, Durham, 7 July 1628, deprived and imprisoned; **Prynne** and **Burton** vs. Cosin's *Collection of Private Devotions*). Authoritative history: **Kenneth Fincham & Nicholas Tyacke, *Altars Restored* (OUP, 2007)**. And RJ's Revelation-as-liturgy reading has a recognizable modern provenance: **Scott Hahn, *The Lamb's Supper: The Mass as Heaven on Earth* (1999)**, echoing John Paul II's "mysterious participation in the heavenly liturgy" — a *Roman* line, not an Anglican-formulary one, worth engaging as the steel-man. **Cross-ref §12:** the bronze-serpent datum (incense — *qiṭṭēr* — burned to a God-commanded object, condemned and the object destroyed: 2 Kings 18:4) links the incense lever here to the images question in §12.

- **Instruments and contemporary songs are adiaphora (GV-28).** Contemporary instruments (guitars, drums) and songs are "not in and of themselves a problem." **[Stated, GV-28]** **[Analysis]** Answers a standing open question: instruments are adiaphora for him (no strict-RPW exclusion), which *isolates* the extra theological freight he loads specifically onto incense (cf. `RJ_Incense_Analysis`). If guitars are indifferent circumstances but incense is a commanded/signifying element, the asymmetry is itself a question.
- **Worship's aim is God, not entertainment (GV-29) — common ground.** Worship must aim at God, not entertainment; a man-centered focus "is idolatry." He even concedes high-church vestments *can* be misused to "impress … people," and cites the catechumen dismissal (Liturgy of the Sacrament). **[Stated, GV-29]** **[Analysis]** Partial Bucket-B *common ground* (God-centered worship; cf. §15) — **not** a lever. The vestments-can-impress concession is a useful candor datum.

### BP batch — "Responding to Matthew Everhard on the Regulative Principle," full video (BP-50 through BP-60)

*Continues the BP-35–49 single-video data set logged immediately above; same source, same current-voice register. BP-56 intentionally not used — see Changelog for this pass.*

- ★ **Christmas/Easter consistency claim against Everhard, exact wording (BP-50).** RJ speculates aloud, unprompted, about whether Everhard observes the church calendar at all: "I actually am, by the way, wondering if he celebrates Easter and Christmas. I would say his principles have to bar him from at least celebrating Christmas and probably Easter as well." Presented as RJ's own inference about what Everhard's stated RPW position entails, not as something RJ has confirmed Everhard holds or said. **[Stated, BP-RPW]**
  - **[Analysis]** Conflates two categories the RPW (WCF 21.1) actually separates: (1) the elements of worship offered to God and (2) the occasion/calendar on which an unchanged set of elements is exercised. A congregation gathering on December 25 to preach, pray, and sing about the incarnation, with no new element introduced and no obligation imposed on conscience, does not violate a standard RPW reading merely by the topical occasion of the gathering. RJ's claim would only hold against a stronger, specifically Puritan/Sabbatarian anti-festival position, not against RPW-as-such, and not necessarily against Everhard's own stated view, which RJ does not quote or cite here.
  - **[Analysis — relationship to BP-41]** BP-41 already logs Hanukkah/synagogue/Lord's-Day-shift as RJ's general wedge against a strict-imperative RPW caricature; the existing rebuttal (WCF 21.1's three-source test, element/circumstance split) already absorbs that wedge. BP-50 is narrower: not a counter-example to the RPW in the abstract, but an unverified claim about a specific named interlocutor's position, used to discredit him before textual engagement begins.
  - **[Analysis — register]** Informal/polemical register (live reaction stream, explicitly speculative: "I actually am... wondering if"), not a settled teaching-context claim. Tag and treat accordingly per the project's register-dating convention; remains fair to raise since RJ said it publicly about a named individual.

- **John 10 / Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah) textual gap (BP-51).** RJ states: "the other example I like to give is, I think, was John 10, where Jesus is celebrating Hanukkah. Hanukkah is not an Old Testament liturgical feast day... It comes from the Maccabees... Yet Jesus himself is going to it," repeated later: "Again, you look at the Feast of Booths or Hanukkah. Jesus himself goes to it in what I think John 10." **[Stated, BP-RPW]**
  - **[Analysis]** John 10:22-23 states only that "the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem... and Jesus was walking in the temple, in the portico of Solomon." Records geographic presence and a subsequent dispute (10:24-39); does not narrate participation in any feast-distinctive rite, comment on the feast's legitimacy, or indicate approval/institution. RJ's characterization ("Jesus is celebrating Hanukkah," "going to it") overstates textual support: presence during a feast is not the same as celebrating it, and is weaker still as dominical warrant for the church's liberty to institute new feasts. "Jesus didn't condemn it" is an argument from silence, notably weaker than his explicit condemnation of temple commerce in John 2.
  - **[Analysis — relationship to BP-41]** BP-41 lists Hanukkah as one item in a three-item wedge list, absorbed by WCF 1.6's element/circumstance split (an OT liturgical-calendar addition, not a claim about NT dominical institution). BP-51 isolates a different, sharper problem specific to Hanukkah alone: whether the cited text even supports the factual claim RJ makes about what Jesus did. A textual/exegetical-accuracy lever, distinct from the element/circumstance-taxonomy lever.

- ★ **The Fourth of July reductio against the RPW, exact wording (BP-52).** Same rhetorical move as BP-50, run against the RPW generally rather than against Everhard by name: "now what you're saying is that the fourth of july is... perfectly fine to gather together with your christian friends over... although... I guess we're not allowed to pray when we get together for that." Generalizes to a broader complaint that RPW proponents would have to "take God out of" Christmas, Valentine's Day, and Thanksgiving to permit them. **[Stated, BP-RPW]**
  - **[Analysis]** Same structural problem as BP-50: an inference about what "what you're saying is," not a quotation of any actual RPW proponent holding that private/family prayer on a non-liturgical occasion is forbidden. The RPW regulates the corporate, official worship of the visible church (its appointed elements, in its appointed assemblies), not whether individual Christians may pray at a family gathering. Conflates (1) the church corporately instituting a new liturgical feast with its own propers/calendar status and (2) private or family prayer on a day with no ecclesial status — the RPW speaks to the former, not the latter. No Reformed RPW proponent, historically or currently, has held private prayer unlawful on secular holidays.
  - **[Analysis — pattern note]** BP-50 and BP-52 share a recurring form: characterizing an opposing position via an unattributed "what you're saying is" inference, then critiquing the inference rather than a sourced statement from an actual interlocutor. Worth tracking as a standing pattern across the corpus, not a one-off.

- ★★ **Fallacy diagnosis — the "concede-then-reclaim" move on Malachi 1:11 (BP-53).** Builds on BP-38/BP-39 (raw quotes already on file) by naming the argument's logical structure. Sequence: (1) demand justification for reading Malachi 1:11 "spiritually" — "I'm going to ask for your justification for that spiritualizing"; (2) appear to concede the spiritual reading — "Let's say Malachi 1.11 is actually about a spiritual thing... Let's just even give that to them"; (3) immediately reclaim physical incense as warranted anyway via an unargued premise — "An image doesn't work if it's not being used. It has to be used for it to work. So we should be using it for worship." **[Stated, BP-RPW — quotes per BP-38/39]**
  - **[Analysis — the fallacy named]** Step 3 does not follow from step 2. "Malachi 1:11 functions as a typological/spiritual image" and "the church must liturgically reenact the image's literal referent for the image to function" are different claims; the second requires an independent argument RJ never supplies. He asserts "an image doesn't work if it's not being used" as if self-evident, but this contradicts ordinary typological function: a type's meaning is conveyed through the text and fulfilled in its antitype without requiring the type's literal referent to be physically reenacted (the golden lampstand and the ark in Revelation are not literally reinstituted as furniture; they function as image without reenactment). Best named as a hidden/unargued premise doing the work of a conclusion (a form of begging the question), wrapped in the rhetorical shape of a fair-minded concession.
  - **[Analysis — self-inconsistency lever, stronger than the prior framing]** RJ does not apply his own "the image needs a literal referent to work" rule to the rest of the very verse he's citing. Malachi 1:11 pairs "incense" with "a pure offering" in synonymous parallelism. If the rule licenses physical incense, identical logic licenses/requires a literal sacrificial offering on an altar, since "pure offering" is exactly as imagistic/typological as "incense" within the same clause. RJ does not do this (he affirms, per BP-43, that incense is "not trying to earn God's favor," i.e. explicitly non-sacrificial/non-propitiatory) — meaning he applies his own interpretive rule selectively to the one clause supporting his existing practice and tacitly abandons it for the parallel clause that would not. Stronger and cleaner than a cross-tradition dispute: requires no imported Reformed presupposition, only that RJ apply his own stated method evenly within a single verse.
  - **[Analysis — burden of proof, reversed]** RJ frames the burden as resting on whoever reads Malachi 1:11 typologically rather than as a literal NT-era command. Given his own stated fulfillment hermeneutic elsewhere in this corpus ("the principle of high churchness is never rescinded... there are particular things that are rescinded in Hebrews," BP-40) and the shadow-substance abrogation axis already established (Col 2:16-17; Heb 10:1), the more defensible default for OT cultic/ceremonial language in a NT-era reading is the opposite: presumptively fulfilled/typological unless a positive NT warrant establishes continued physical performance. JD's framing (June 2026): the burden is at minimum shared, arguably RJ's, to show why this particular ceremonial type-image alone should be read as requiring continued physical performance rather than fulfillment.
  - **[Analysis — relationship to existing material]** Does not introduce a new quote-level data point; supplies the missing logical-structure analysis for BP-38/39. Read as BP-53's analytical companion. Recommend any future drafting of Q4a incorporate the "pure offering" parallel-clause inconsistency as the lead move.

- ★ **The "Puritan statue vs. statue of Christ" reductio against Everhard (BP-54).** RJ reads and endorses a viewer chat comment ("Form in the Fire"), then extends it himself: "Reminds me of those in our culture who are chill with venerating our fallen soldiers, but think statues of saints are idolatry... you'll notice he's got some Puritan... a statue of the Puritan. He would not have a statue of our Lord, though, I'm sure. And I... find that kind of frustrating because... we cannot apparently... proclaim the wonder of our Lord, but we can proclaim the wonder of our particular theologians that we like." **[Stated, BP-RPW — mixed source: initiating line from named chat commenter, extended/endorsed by RJ in the same breath]**
  - **[Analysis — the equivocation, JD-identified]** Collapses three categories a standard Reformed second-commandment position (WLC 109; the historic objection targets depicting the divine nature, not representational art of human beings as such) keeps separate: (1) memorial statues of historic, non-divine human figures — no live second-commandment question under any mainstream Reformed reading; (2) statues of saints in a devotional/liturgical setting, where the question is documented cultic FUNCTION (veneration, invocation, votive use), not the bare existence of an image; (3) an attempted image of Christ specifically, raising the distinct objection that the invisible, infinite divine nature cannot be reduced to a physical representation at all. RJ's reductio only generates its "gotcha" by treating (1) and (3) as the same kind of case. A Presbyterian declining a statue of Christ while keeping a Puritan bust is not inconsistent by any standard Reformed criterion; the cases are governed by different principles.
  - **[Analysis — the saints category, correctly distinguished]** Category (2) is the one place a substantive question exists, and it is function/context, not same-as-Christ: a Reformed Christian could consistently permit a statue of a historic Christian figure as art/memorial while objecting to its placement and use as an object of veneration in worship — that liturgical function, not the bare image, is the actual target of the Reformed objection. Tracks the circumstance-vs-element distinction already developed elsewhere in this project (statue in a library = circumstance/adornment; statue receiving liturgical veneration = element requiring positive warrant).
  - **[Analysis — "proclaim the wonder of our Lord" specifically]** JD's observation is the theological crux: God (and the divine nature of Christ) is by definition invisible and uncircumscribable, so a physical statue cannot "proclaim the wonder" of the divine nature, only a sculptor's imagination of an incarnate body's appearance. This is the substance of WLC 109's prohibition on "making any representation of God... whether of all or of any of the three persons," and is not answerable by pointing to permitted memorial statues of non-divine human beings.
  - **[Cross-reference flag]** Possible natural home alongside existing §12 icons material (Q17/Q18); left in §13 per source chronology, cross-link at JD's discretion.

- ★ **The Wednesday-meeting tu quoque against Everhard (BP-55).** "that makes me wonder what happens on a Wednesday. Cause like every church I know, almost every church I know meets for like a Wednesday evening thing. Are they saying that it's sinful? Like do the Presbyterians of his sort worship together on Wednesday evenings every week or have a men's Bible study or something like that. And then do they pray? Or do they say, nope, you're not allowed to pray?" **[Stated, BP-RPW]**
  - **[Analysis — category error, same family as BP-50/BP-52]** Conflates the RPW's regulation of the ELEMENTS of corporate worship with the OCCASION/frequency of a gathering at which already-warranted elements occur. A Wednesday Bible study introduces no new element; it is the same warranted activities exercised on an ordinary, non-liturgically-marked day, with no claim to ecclesial/episcopal authority. The disanalogy tracks the element/circumstance line already developed in this project (cf. BP-41's master framing note). No Reformed RPW proponent holds prayer/Bible study forbidden on non-Sundays; the rhetorical question targets a position no one holds — the same pattern flagged in BP-50 and BP-52.
  - **[Analysis — pattern note, cross-reference]** Third instance in a single video of the same underlying move (BP-50, BP-52, BP-55): an unattributed or loosely-attributed "your principle would have to mean X" claim, where X is not something any actual RPW proponent holds, built on collapsing the element/occasion (or element/circumstance) distinction. Recommend treating this trio as a single named pattern at reconcile rather than three independent rhetorical quirks.

- ★ **Calendar-latitude argument elides apostolic-practice vs. unattested-institution distinction (BP-57).** [Note: BP-56 intentionally not used — see changelog entry below.] "we see that there are liturgical calendars that are made within the Old Testament that they are actually added to... we see them going to the synagogues, even though there's not a command... There's no explicit command to change from Saturday to Sunday, the Lord's Day... we have, as the church, understood these commands of God to worship and made a calendar from it. That is not, I think, opposed to the regulative principle of worship." **[Stated, BP-RPW]**
  - **[Analysis]** Elides a distinction between two kinds of "addition." The Lord's-Day shift and weekly-gathering rhythm have a claimed warrant in apostolic example (Acts 20:7; 1 Cor 16:2), which standard Reformed method (WCF 1.6's "good and necessary consequence") treats as functionally normative even without an explicit verbal command — recognizing an apostolically-attested practice, not inventing one. Ash Wednesday, Lent, and a fixed annual liturgical Easter/Christmas have no equivalent claim to apostolic-practice precedent; later ecclesiastical institutions with no claimed first-century attestation. RJ's argument treats "the church has always exercised some calendar-shaping liberty" as licensing unlimited further institution, without addressing the warrant-tier difference between recognizing an apostolically-attested practice and instituting an unattested new one. Structurally the same move as BP-55, applied at the institutional/calendar level rather than the weekly-frequency level.

- ★★ **The "condemnable act" extrapolation against Everhard (BP-58).** "maybe Pastor Everhard wouldn't say that the people who do this are damned to hell, but that it's a condemnable act to actually worship God with Easter services and Christmas and having all these other things. I think that's just incredibly problematic." **[Stated, BP-RPW]**
  - **[Analysis — JD-identified]** Note the explicit hedge ("maybe Pastor Everhard wouldn't say") — RJ knowingly extrapolating, not quoting; more candid than BP-50 but shares its structure. The likely actual Reformed RPW objection to Ash Wednesday is institutional/categorical: the church should not institute an unwarranted new liturgical rite — a claim about ecclesial propriety, not about an individual worshipper's moral status. RJ collapses "the church should not institute this" into "anyone who worships there has committed a condemnable act," which does not follow from a bare RPW commitment and is not a position Everhard is shown to hold. A more careful Reformed objection would likely turn on Ash Wednesday introducing a new religious rite (imposition of ashes as a distinct ceremonial element) rather than objecting to gathering/worship on a non-Sunday as such — a distinction RJ's framing does not register. Charity failure independent of whether the underlying RPW dispute is otherwise correctly characterized.

- ★★ **The "arrogance" charge against the Reformation as a whole — retrieval vs. innovation, JD's strongest point in this batch (BP-59).** "I think ultimately at the end of the day the position itself is arrogant... it just seems very arrogant to say the entire church got it wrong, uh, whether it be the episcopate [or the calendar]... That in and of itself is arrogant." (Companion raw quote already on file at BP-46.) **[Stated, BP-RPW]**
  - **[Analysis — JD-identified, recommend high priority]** Unstated premise: the Reformers' claim took the form "we discovered something new that 1,500 years of Christians missed." Misdescribes the magisterial Reformers' actual self-understanding: retrieval, not innovation — appeal to Scripture and apostolic/patristic-era practice against later medieval accretions (Calvin's prefatory address to Francis I in the Institutes explicitly appeals to the ancient church and the fathers against contemporary Rome, arguing Rome had departed from antiquity). The actual classical Reformed argument was never "the entire church was wrong for 1,500 years and we alone got it right," but "received apostolic practice was overlaid with unwarranted later accretion, and we are recovering the earlier standard."
  - **[Analysis — mirror-image self-application, the sharpest form of this point]** RJ uses, against the Reformers, exactly the charge (illegitimate prideful innovation against received tradition) Rome has historically leveled against the Reformation, while relying on the mirror-image defense (retrieval of apostolic/patristic practice against later Reformed "neutering") for his own incense, calendar, and episcopacy positions elsewhere in this corpus. If "claiming the wider church got something wrong" is inherently arrogant, the charge applies with equal force to RJ's own claims against the Reformed tradition's abandonment of incense, vestments, and the church calendar; if not inherently arrogant when done with a retrieval-claim and textual/historical argument, the same standard should extend to the Reformers' parallel retrieval-claim. Recommend-elevate: does not depend on any contested Reformed doctrinal premise, only on the historical accuracy of how the Reformers characterized their own project — close to a pure consistency lever.
  - **[Analysis — secondary tension, RJ's own RPW commitment]** RJ self-identifies as an RPW proponent ("I would say I'm doing that rather consistently") while attacking, as inherently arrogant, the foundational move (claiming a long-standing majority church practice was mistaken and correcting it) that any RPW commitment, including a narrower Anglo-Catholic one, necessarily requires at some point relative to medieval Western liturgical practice he himself rejects. Lower-priority secondary tension.

- **BCP/Puritans generalization, closing claim (BP-60).** "the Puritans, they hated the BCP. In fact, many of them were just like, no, we don't want any liturgy... So it is really interesting that people like the Reverend Everhart [sic]... are fierce proponents of the regulative principle [and] also really have a great love and respect for the prayer book, because the prayer book was target number one for many of the Puritans." Notably hedged: "I'm not trying to sort of call him a hypocrite or anything like that." **[Stated, BP-RPW]**
  - **[Analysis]** Generalizes a genuinely diverse historical landscape into a monolith. Post-Reformation Reformed/Puritan attitudes toward set liturgical forms varied considerably; the more precise claim is that the Westminster Directory for Public Worship (1645) replaced the BCP with a directory model in the specific, politically-charged context of mid-seventeenth-century conflict over an imposed, uniform liturgy, not a uniform Puritan rejection of liturgy-as-genre. Continental Reformed and some English/Scottish worship retained structured liturgical forms (Calvin's Geneva liturgy; the Scottish Book of Common Order); much of the historic objection centered on specific contested ceremonial elements within the BCP (vestments, kneeling at communion, the sign of the cross in baptism) rather than fixed-form liturgy as such. Fairness note: RJ explicitly disclaims the "hypocrite" framing before making the point — distinguishes this finding's register from the sharper-edged reductios earlier in the same video.

- **Pattern-level cross-reference note.** BP-50, BP-52, BP-55, BP-57, and BP-58 share a recurring structural form across this single video: characterizing an opposing position via inference ("what you're saying is," "his principles have to mean," "maybe he wouldn't say X but Y follows") rather than via direct citation of the interlocutor's own stated view, generally by collapsing a real distinction (element/occasion, apostolic-attested practice/unattested institution, institutional propriety/individual culpability). BP-59 is the structurally most significant finding in the batch: same pattern operating at the foundational, methodological level (the propriety of correcting long-standing majority church practice at all) rather than a single local dispute, and without requiring any contested Reformed doctrinal premise.

- **[JD aside — explicitly NOT a sourced finding, retained for internal context only, not for use in conversation with RJ].** JD's own unconfirmed working hypothesis: this pattern (treating RPW positions as requiring more than anyone actually holds) may trace to RJ's own upbringing in a fundamentalist Baptist household with an exclusivist "only true church" self-conception. Not a claim RJ has made about himself in any source reviewed to date. Per the project's discipline against psychoanalyzing motivations without a stated basis, this should not be raised with RJ directly or treated as an explanatory finding. Retained only for JD's private calibration.


### Revelation class, 2026 (RV batch) — vantage point, incense-as-act, and the intelligibility constraint

> ⚠️ **READ THIS FIRST: THE STANDING OBSTACLE IS NOT MOVED BY THIS BATCH.** DQ-9 (act-level versus principle-level warrant) is nowhere stated, defended, bounded or qualified in the 2026 sessions. **He never mentions the regulative principle at all in this batch** — zero occurrences of "regulative," zero of the "regular principle" ASR variant, zero of "principle of worship." The only bearing is indirect and hermeneutical, and it lives in §18 (RV-2, RV-11), where it **sharpens a fork rather than resolving one**.

- **★ He frames the whole of Revelation as seen from INSIDE heavenly worship (RV-3).** *"remember Saint John is seeing all of this from this worship that is happening, this heavenly worship from that room that that great hall of worship that's happening. He's seeing all this stuff happen through worship."* Said in passing, as an aside, while explaining Revelation 11:19. **[Stated, RV-3]** **[Stated-Analysis]** This is the **vantage-point claim** a heavenly-liturgy-as-template argument needs, now on record for the 2026 class as well as the 2025 one (cf. Rev-11 below). It is stated as a fact about the vision's setting, and **he draws no liturgical inference from it here** — he moves straight on to the ark and the theophany. Cross-ref DQ-15, DQ-7, RV-22.
- **★ Incense on an altar described THREE TIMES as the act by which pagan worship was performed and certified (RV-20).** *"give a little bit of incense onto the altar for the gods or for Caesar, right? Worship Caesar. Worship the gods. We don't care if you believe in them or not."* / *"As long as you had all of the emperor's gods in your little idol in your little altar section of your of your house, they were fine with it."* / *"As long as you put a little bit of incense on the altar once a year, whatever, they were fine with it."* And on the *libelli*: *"This is where there are certificates that are given showing that you uh did your quote civic duty to put incense on the altar to worship the gods."* **[Stated, RV-20]**
  - **[Analysis] TWO READINGS, BOTH LIVE, NEITHER CHOSEN.** **(a) The act carries the worship.** On his own telling the required thing was the *placing of incense on an altar*; belief was explicitly not required ("We don't care if you believe in them or not"), and the certificate attested the **act**. That is an **act-level account of what constitutes an act of worship, from his own mouth, in a context with no polemical stake**, and it sits against DQ-9's principle-level substitution. **(b) The object carries the worship.** What made it worship was that the altar was a *pagan* altar and the recipient a *false god*, so the act-level reading proves nothing about incense as such.
  - ⚠️ **Reading (b) is strong and is very likely what he would say. DO NOT log (a) as though it were established.** ⚠️ **He is describing pagan practice and says nothing whatever about Christian liturgical incense in this session.** The value of the datum is that it is **his**, it requires **no contested Reformed premise**, and it is **portable**. Cross-ref DQ-4, DQ-7, question-list items 1 and 21.
- **★★ An AUDIENCE-INTELLIGIBILITY CONSTRAINT on visionary content, stated as his reason for rejecting futurism (RV-22).** *"the book of Revelation itself is written to these seven churches and it's there for them for them to look at these uh to read these things and to watch for these things to happen"*; *"The idea is that this is a book that is meant also for us but it has to make sense to them too"*; *"St. John did not know about microchips. He did not see a vision of microchips."* Developed at length via a Presbyterian minister's joke about a Christian in Antioch who identifies the beast and then cannot identify the modern politician. On 666 he is emphatic that the number *"is meant for them to understand the exact person being talked about."* **[Stated, RV-22]**
  - **[Analysis] — the batch's strongest DQ-15 material.** He has stated, **unprompted and for his own eschatological purposes**, that the images given to St. John had to be intelligible to the first-century recipients as referring to their own situation, and **he uses that constraint to rule readings out.** He applies it to beasts, numbers and empires. **He does not apply it to the worship imagery.** ⚠️ **Whether it should apply there is the project's argument, not his statement.** ⚠️ **The reply available to him is obvious and should be anticipated rather than discovered later:** heavenly worship imagery was intelligible to first-century readers *precisely because they knew temple worship* — a continuity answer, and not an evasion.
- **Appeal to visions listed as a marker of heretical movements, with Colossians 2:18 read aloud in the class (RV-21).** *"This points to false signs that mimic prophetic authority in order to deceive us."* / *"Heretical movements often claim visions, miracles, prophecies, secret knowledge, or extraordinary spiritual manifestations."* **[Stated, RV-21]** Earlier in the same session he had a parishioner read Colossians 2:18-23 aloud, including, verbatim as read, *"Taking his stand on visions he has seen inflated without cause by his fleshly mind."* He offers no comment on that clause and moves on to Gnosticism generally. ⚠️ **ATTRIBUTION CARE: the Colossians text is scripture read by a parishioner, not RJ speaking.** It is logged as context for what was before the class, **not** as his statement; **the tag attaches to his own two sentences only.** **[Analysis]** The distinction he is drawing is between *canonical* vision and *claimed extra-canonical* vision, and that distinction is perfectly available to him. **It does not by itself embarrass a heavenly-liturgy argument.** What it does is put on record that he treats "I saw it in a vision" as needing a **further warrant** before it authorizes anything — which is the shape DQ-15 is probing. ⚠️ **Do not run this as a contradiction. It is not one.**

> ⭐⭐ **THE FAST DISCIPLINE, STATED AS THE PARISH'S OWN AND IN HIS OWN FIRST PERSON (`IP-61`).** **Every Friday, all year**, is a fasting day — *"which is no meat"* — with **one exception, possibly two: a Friday falling between Christmas and Epiphany.** **Ash Wednesday and Good Friday** are the two total fasts, *"the bookends."* In Lent the practice is **one meal plus two smaller eatings that do not themselves constitute a full meal, daily, apart from Sundays**; **Sundays are not fast days** *"at least once communion is done"*; and **before communion the expectation is a total fast from food — *"that's at least the priest, but also the parishioners tend to do it as well."*** ⭐⭐ **AND THE ENFORCEMENT POSTURE IS STATED AS PLAINLY AS THE RULE: he announces the fast day and then does not police it — *"I don't go around asking people, have you been fasting today?"* — and describes eating a salad opposite a parishioner's ham sandwich on a Lenten Friday without comment.**

- BCP history (AW-II): Cranmer compiles from the Sarum Rite + Eastern/Western liturgies; 1549 (traditional) and 1552 (reformed) both "reformed and Catholic"; 1662 the standard; American line via Seabury/Scottish Episcopal Church (hence the epiclesis and a more "traditional" American tradition); 1928 → his book; 1979 a radical, theologically-compromised departure. **[Stated, AW-II]**  
- **1928 BCP preference, dated to the deacon era (RC-1).** Prefers the 1928 BCP ("more Catholic minded than elements of the 1662"), though licensed to use the 2019, and "uses both." Partly answers D8/G9: the preference is at least partly substantive, not merely jurisdictional, and was already in place before St. Francis. Teaches the 1928 BCP Mass at St. Francis as of 2025 (RC-3). **[Stated, RC1-14, RC3-1]**
- **BCP sources, additional nuance (RC-3).** Confirms the BCP draws from the Sarum Rite plus Eastern and Western liturgies, and credits the Reformation's simplification of over-complicated ceremonial for lay participation, a nuance against the RC1-11 "we want more ceremonies" emphasis (§10): over-complication is the target, not healthy ceremonial as such. **[Stated, RC3-5]**
- **Ember and Lent practice, 2025 (RC-3).** Observes ember-day fasts and Lent ("our penitential season"); drops the Gloria and Alleluia in Lent and Advent; confirms the Lent-as-wilderness-fast frame ("the 40 days in the wilderness … with Christ in the desert"). **[Stated, RC3-14, RC3-29]**
- **Deuterocanon read in worship (RC-4).** The 1928 lectionary reads the deuterocanon in worship (Wisdom, Tobit); his home parish marks the distinction with "here ends the reading." **[Stated, RC4-2]**
- ⚠️ **Cranmer claim:** asserts Cranmer revised 1549→1552 under *political pressure*, not conviction (cites Toon; Alan Jacobs; quotes the 1552 Act of Uniformity calling 1549 "agreeable to the Word of God"). **[Stated, AW-II]** **Correction [Analysis]:** mainstream scholarship — Diarmaid MacCulloch, *Thomas Cranmer: A Life* (1996) — holds Cranmer's eucharistic theology genuinely moved Reformed (via Bucer, Vermigli) across 1548–52, so the 1552 reflects his settled mature mind, not coercion. This undercuts a "1549 is the real Anglicanism" framing if he leans on it. Other history is largely sound (missa/dismissal etymology; Athanasian Creed's late 5th–6th-c. date; Nicene Creed's later entry into the liturgy). Minor: "Ember \< quatuor tempora" is one hypothesis; OE *ymbryne* is the more standard derivation.  
- Morning/Evening Prayer: a priest's daily duty; the Reformation turned the medieval daily *re-sacrifice* into daily *prayer* as the priest's offering; laity may pray all but the Absolution; wants to revive daily public Offices. 30-day Psalter; King James for lessons, Coverdale for the Psalter (for chantability). **[Stated, AW-II/III, Recon-Euch]**  
- Communion structure (AW-IV/V): Liturgy of the Word (incl. Decalogue/Summary of the Law — law/gospel) → Gospel as the climax (not the homily) → Creed → ~15-min homily → Liturgy of the Sacrament (Offertory → Prayer for the Church → Confession/Absolution/Comfortable Words → Sursum Corda/Sanctus → Consecration incl. words of institution as essential + oblation + epiclesis/invocation → Communion → Thanksgiving → Gloria → Benediction). Defends the epiclesis as fine though not strictly necessary (J. I. Packer anecdote). **[Stated, AW-IV/V, Recon-Euch]**  
- **Pre–Vatican II calendar:** Advent → Christmas (12 days) → Epiphany → Gesima Sundays → Lent → Holy Week → Easter (50 days) → Ascension (Thursday, kept on the day) → Whitsuntide/Pentecost → Trinity. Counts from Trinity, not "after Pentecost." The calendar is for "walking with Christ" through the year. **[Stated, AW-VI, Lent vid]**  
- **Ember Days:** fasting + prayer + a letter to the bishop on one's spiritual state; **required of priests/deacons, laity encouraged**. **[Stated, AW-VI, Ember vid]**  
- **Lent:** 40 days (Sundays not counted); total fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday (as health allows); abstinence from meat and dairy, with fish (and historically beaver) as exceptions; a "Lenten discipline" = give up a lawful good + take on a positive practice (e.g., the whole Psalter weekly). Defends imposition of ashes against the Matt 6:16 objection via a **public-fast** warrant (Joel 2:12–17), carefully distinguishing private from public fasting and explicitly granting the sin is ostentation, not visibility. **[Stated, AW-VI, Lent vid]**  
- **[Analysis]** The Reformed tradition rejects holy days/fasts that *bind the conscience* beyond the Lord's Day (WCF 21; Westminster Directory; Col 2:16–23 "will-worship"; Gal 4:9–11). His Matt 6:16 handling is fair — don't attack it. The pressure point is the leap from "public fasts existed" (Joel 2 is a one-off national emergency) to "an annually imposed, dietary-ruled Lent," plus the conscience-binding implied by "required of the clergy."  
- **[Analysis — elevated in v0.8, from the Lent/Ash Wednesday video transcript]** Lent moves from a down-weighted reserve item to an **active question** (list Q14), because the video gives two *RJ-specific* hooks rather than the generic calendar objection. (1) **Conscience-binding edge:** he frames the historic fast as expected/mandated (exceptions only for the sick, elderly, young) — so the internal-Anglican question is whether the formulary's Table of Fasts *binds* conscience or *commends* a discipline. (2) **The category leaps in his Matt 6 / Joel 2 reasoning** (this is the live purchase, not "you misread Matt 6"): Joel 2 / Jonah / 2 Chron 20 are *ad hoc* national-emergency convocations, never annually scheduled; the wilderness fast he takes as Lent's *model* was itself solitary, concealed, and a unique *once-for-all messianic* event (Christ recapitulating Israel's forty years), not a yearly template; and "keep the ashes on as a public witness" sits awkwardly against "wash your face, that you appear not unto men to fast." (3) **Dating correction (he says preparation goes back to the 2nd century):** *true for a short fast* — Irenaeus (c. 190, in Eusebius, *Church History* 5.24) describes a pre-Easter fast of "one day, two days, or forty *hours*," varying by region — but the **40-day season is 4th-century** (Athanasius, *Festal Letters*, 331). And the kicker: Irenaeus cites that 2nd-century *variety* precisely to argue Pope Victor should **not** break communion over it — so the earliest evidence is a witness *for liberty*, against binding conscience to a uniform fast. (The "forty days" reading of Irenaeus is **Rufinus's** late-4th-c. mistranslation, which modern scholarship rejects.) Still don't *open* with Lent; the generic calendar difference stays secondary, but these give real, primary-source-grounded purchase if it arises. Tell in pocket: even Doug Wilson doesn't observe Lenten seasons.
- **Worship as God-directed formation, not entertainment (BP-33).** "I am going to worship not to get something out of it but specifically because I am wanting to be formed by it"; sharp critique of "concert venue" megachurch worship — confirms the existing §13 anti-entertainment finding. Drawn to Anglican worship's beauty: iconography, incense, and AD ORIENTEM ("the priest is facing the same direction as all the people") — ad orientem confirms the existing §10 finding; this is the same datum from an earlier source. Prefers the 1928 US BCP for traditional/Elizabethan language over 1979 TEC/2019 ACNA — consistent with the already-dated 1928 preference (RC, deacon era); rationale given here is aesthetic/traditional-language (bears on D8/D9). **[Stated, BP-Angl]**
- **Conservative-retention default, sharpened (BP-34).** Confirms and sharpens the existing conservative-retention disposition (IP-2/IP-9) as consistent rather than ad hoc. Defends liturgy against "vain repetition" (ABCs analogy: "why are we fiddling with something that works"); affirms both liturgical AND extemporaneous prayer as "needed." ## 15. Where He's Sound (common ground — credit it)

- Soteriology largely Reformed-friendly: law/gospel, sola fide, union with Christ, Rom 6 against antinomianism, functional third use. **[Stated, AW-I/IV]**  
- Rejects transubstantiation and the propitiatory/re-sacrifice Mass; defends communion in both kinds and *against* withholding the cup ("there's never going to be a time when… I will only offer the bread"). **[Stated, AW-V, Recon-Euch]**  
- Will not do a private Mass. **[Stated, AW-V]**  
- Shares the critique of revivalist/entertainment worship; tone irenic and self-aware throughout. **[Stated, AW-I, Recon-Euch]**
- **Additional common-ground items surfaced by the RC set:** always offers both kinds, against withholding the cup (RC3-26); declarative absolution with no priestly "power of his own" (RC3-21); robust sola fide back to the deacon era (RC1-15); ecclesial sola scriptura held under Scripture, bishop, and Church (RC5-3); God-centered, non-crowd-centered worship rationale (RC3-4); the keys-as-discipline reading aligned with the Reformed account (RC7-5); and a consistent, self-correcting intellectual-honesty and sourcing discipline visible across the papacy material (RC7-3, RC7-10, RC2-2, RC4-7), worth naming as the register the in-person dialogue should aim to match.
- **Real-presence reinforcement (BP-18).** One who "stubbornly rejects the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist is still committing a grave sin" — reinforces the high-stakes framing already on record around real presence (§8, Q11). **[Stated, BP-Sac]**

### ⚠️ STRUCTURAL NOTE — read before using this section (added 260725-1)

**This section had not moved since the RC batch, while the tensions sections grew weekly.** Between the RC batch and 260724-2 the corpus added the entire **DQ series (DQ-1 … DQ-15)** — fifteen findings, several of them the strongest material the project has — and **§15 received none of it.** Not because nothing was creditable: the creditable material was logged, and in five cases the analysis block *explicitly said* "credit it (§15)." It was noted and never folded in.

**That asymmetry biases the source-of-truth document by construction.** A file that accumulates tensions weekly and common ground never is not a record of a man's positions; it is a brief against him, and it will read that way to its own author six months from now. The distortion compounds silently, because nothing about a missing entry announces itself.

**The discipline going forward:** every pass sweeps its own new findings for *common ground*, *credit it*, *formulary-faithful*, *no lever here*, and folds them here **in the same pass**. Check **C10** in `validate_project.py` now flags any finding whose analysis marks common ground but which §15 does not cite, and separately flags §15 falling behind the DQ ledger head. **Noted in an analysis block is not logged in §15.**

### DQ-series common ground (added 260725-1)

- **⭐ He affirms the positive-warrant rule itself (DQ-4).** Asked directly whether he holds that acts of worship require positive warrant in Scripture — by command, approved example, or necessary inference — he answered **"Correct,"** and reframed his own position as the RPW "rightly **applied**" rather than a different principle. **[Stated, DQ-4]** **[Analysis]** This is the largest single piece of common ground in the corpus and the reason every subsequent question is intramural. Credit it plainly and often: the disagreement is about the filter on warrant sources, not about whether warrant is needed.

- **⭐ He affirms material sufficiency, in his own words (DQ-12).** *"The Scriptures alone are infallible and materially sufficient for the essential doctrines of the Faith."* **[Stated, DQ-12]** Volunteered in the course of conceding that he **cannot populate a second tier** of required-but-unprovable beliefs: everything he could think of relocated into "provable from Scripture, though not to everyone's satisfaction." **[Stated, DQ-12]** **[Analysis]** This forecloses a whole class of sola-scriptura arguments as simply inapplicable to him, and it was stated **against his own interest**, unprompted, in answer to a question probing for the opposite. It also matters beyond this project — it belongs in the `A Protestant Defense of the Reformation` workstream.

- **Catechetical prerequisites and the confirmation account (DQ-13).** Confirmation is a *strengthening* rather than a first reception of the Spirit ("One is not going from not having the Holy Ghost to having the Holy Ghost"); the age range is typically 8-12; and the child is expected to know the **Apostles' Creed, the Decalogue, the Two Great Commandments, the Lord's Prayer**, and the basics of the two Dominical sacraments, per the 1928 Offices of Instruction and Catechism. **[Stated, DQ-13]** **[Analysis]** Formulary-standard and unremarkable, and the prerequisite list is a conspicuous place where he is **manifestly not Roman**. No lever here; credit it.

- **⭐ Invocation: all address directed to God (DQ-7, DQ-7a).** His stated position is *"We should, in directing our prayers to God, ask Him that He have the Saints in Heaven pray for us"* — a formulation he claims as his own and reports Trent Horn later adopting. **[Stated, DQ-7a]** **[Analysis]** **Article 22-compatible.** The Article condemns the *invocation* of saints, address directed **to** them; his formulation directs all address to God. This **narrows rather than contradicts** his earlier "I do not find a principle in Scripture that would allow for prayers to the Saints." ⛔ **Common ground, not a lever. Do not run it.**

- **He excludes prayers to the saints, and on the right ground (DQ-10).** *"What blocks my usage of prayers to the Saints in Heaven is that prayer is always seen as an act of worship and as directed to God alone."* **[Stated, DQ-10]** **[Analysis]** That is the Reformed reason, stated in Reformed terms, and it is worth saying so to him. *(Its separate analytical significance — that the exclusion is produced by a rule about the object of worship rather than by his imagery principle — belongs to the tensions material and does not diminish the agreement itself.)*

- **⭐ Grammatical precision as method (DQ-7a).** On Rev 5:8 he rests a worship conclusion on a case ending: the phrase is *προσευχαὶ τῶν ἁγίων*, **τῶν** is genitive, "of the," and "cannot be rightly translated as 'to the' (that would be τοῖς)"; had John written "to the," it *would* be a strong passage for prayers to the saints. **[Stated, DQ-7a]** **[Analysis]** He read the text with maximum precision and **refused an inference the words would not bear, against a conclusion his own tradition would have welcomed.** That is a register note as much as a datum: it is the standard the project asks him to apply elsewhere, and it should be named as *his* standard, not introduced as an external one.

- **⭐ His own OT-carryover examples model fulfilment, not carryover (DQ-8).** Asked how he decides what transfers from the Old Testament, he offered the **Passover Lamb** ("central to our worship") and **"Christ is also our priest"** — both, he said, "strongly in the New Testament." **[Stated, DQ-8]** **[Analysis]** Both are cases where the type terminates in Christ and the antitype is retained. **"Christ is also our priest" concedes that the Levitical priesthood is fulfilled and superseded** — Heb 7:12's substance, granted unprompted, in a neutral context, before incense was ever mentioned. **⚠️ Do not overstate:** he has not stated fulfilment-by-antitype as a general rule and would not accept it as one. The credit is that his own chosen examples are the Reformed pattern.

- **Article 25 answered formulary-faithfully, twice (DQ-2, DQ-11).** He distinguishes the two Dominical/Gospel sacraments from the Five Ecclesial ones, grants the Five "are not of the same level and kind as the Two," and grounds the whole distinction at length in the Second Book of Homilies. **[Stated, DQ-2]** On the grace half he holds the **salvific / non-salvific** line, which is what keeps him inside Article 25's "not of the same level and kind." **[Stated, DQ-11]** **[Analysis]** ⛔ **Both are on the do-not-deploy register.** Pressing further would be pressing him for agreeing with his own formularies.

- **Sourcing discipline, sustained (DQ-1, extending the RC-set note above).** Enumerating the formulary tensions he offered the Article XXIX insertion history, including the 1563 removal and the 1571 reinsertion over Bishop Guest's opposition, and **declined to give exact Homily citations until he had his physical copy to hand.** **[Stated, DQ-1]** **[Analysis]** Consistent with the self-correcting habit already credited from the papacy material. This is the register the dialogue should aim to match.

- **Anti-Nazi / anti-racist stance, at personal cost (IP-11).** He recounts pushing a pro-Nazi parishioner to repent and being reported to the bishop in retaliation; the bishop sided with him. **[Stated, IP-11]** **[Analysis]** Logged in the IP ledger for attribution hygiene and never credited here, which was an omission. It is pastoral courage that cost him something, and a section titled "Where He's Sound" that omits it is not doing its job. *(Added on the 260725-1 audit's own judgment rather than from an existing "credit it" flag — flagged as such.)*

Formulary-faithful; credit it plainly — it is also the shared premise every reconciliation-shaped question in this project relies on.

Credit it sincerely; the open question is scope, not direction.
- **The continuity of prayer itself (DQ-19).** *"Prayer has not fundamentally changed."* **[Stated, DQ-19]** **[Analysis]** True, shared, and worth saying so — the project's own Step 5/5b argument RESTS on prayer continuing (the reality continues; what was fulfilled is the priestly mediation of it). ### `DQ-20`/`DQ-21`/`DQ-22` common ground (added 260833-6) — swept in the SAME pass that logged the findings

- **⭐⭐ Candour about the limits of his own knowledge, on a question he could have answered speculatively (`DQ-22`(c)).** Asked what becomes of one baptized who never heard the Gospel: *"I have no idea what happens with the second half of that."* **[Stated, DQ-22]** **[Analysis]** ⭐ **FILED, and the reasoning is recorded because §15 filings are supposed to be argued rather than assumed.** This is shared ground in the strict sense the `BLOG-16` precedent requires, not merely a likeable trait: **the Reformed answer to the fate of the never-evangelised is also a refusal to pronounce** — the secret things belong to the Lord — so both traditions decline the same question for substantially the same reason. ⭐ **It also belongs to §15's established intellectual-honesty class** (cf. the sourcing-discipline items already filed): he was under no pressure, the speculative answers available to him are cheap, and he declined them unprompted. ⛔ **What is credited is the REFUSAL TO SPECULATE, not any substantive position on the never-evangelised — he states none, and none is implied by filing this.**
- **⭐ The Hebrews ground for the sin offerings, restated (`DQ-20`(a)).** *"There are no sin offerings apart from Christ. Christ is the One Sacrifice to Atone for sins."* **[Stated, DQ-20]** **[Analysis]** The `DQ-18`/`DQ-19` Hebrews item above is hereby **confirmed rather than duplicated** — this is the same shared ground stated a second time, more absolutely, in his own typed words. ⭐ **Worth recording that it did not weaken on restatement.**
- **⭐ Assurance rested on an objective promise rather than on an inward state (`DQ-21`(a)).** *"I have assurance because of the Promises of God given in Baptism."* **[Stated, DQ-21]** **[Analysis]** ⚠️ **FILED NARROWLY AND THE NARROWNESS IS THE POINT.** What is shared is the **anti-introspective instinct** — WCF 18 grounds assurance first in *the divine promises*, and a Reformed reader agrees wholeheartedly that assurance must not rest on the strength of one's own feelings. ⛔ **What is NOT filed, and must not be read into this, is the LOCUS: that the promise is given in baptism, and that baptism is its sole named ground, is precisely where a Reformed reader differs — the `POD-6` decline recorded above governs and is unchanged.** ⭐ **Filing the instinct while declining the locus is the honest form of this item; filing it whole would flatter the section, which `BLOG-16` forbids.**
- **Declines, recorded with reasons:** **(1)** *"Yes, it doesn't necessarily flow from the WCF"* (`DQ-21`(b)) — candid, and creditable as candour, but it is an acknowledgement of **divergence**, and filing a divergence-acknowledgement in the common-ground register is exactly the `BLOG-16` error of putting something here that is not shared ground. **Declined without prejudice to his candour**, which is noted at the finding instead. **(2)** Universal atonement (`DQ-21`(c)) — a genuine cross-tradition difference of the `BLOG-16` Arminianism class, and its interest to this project is evidentiary (Known Gap 4), not irenic; **filing it would also risk reading as approval of a position the project has not examined.** **(3)** Faith and repentance as constituents of the promise (`DQ-22`(b)) — substantively the sharpest divergence in the pass; not common ground on any reading. **(4)** *"The Promises are not for those who reject Christ"* (`DQ-22`(a)) — a stated limit that a Reformed reader would welcome, **but it sits inside the live D10/`BP-29` question and filing it would decide that question by filing**, which the `BLOG-98` precedent forbids. **(5)** The showbread/Eucharist identification (`DQ-20`(b)/(c)) — the pass's headline finding and genuinely impressive as exegesis, **but it is the substance of an open enquiry, not agreed ground; crediting it here would prejudge Step 5c.**

### RV-series common ground (added 260725-4, batch 260725-2)

*⚠️ **Folded in during the SAME pass that logged the tensions**, per the §8 item 4 discipline and the structural note above. Five §15 items came out of one batch; **noted in an analysis block is not logged here**, so they are here.*

- **⭐ He identifies his own position to the class as "partial preterism postmillennial" (RV-1).** *"we're coming from a what's called a partial preterism postmillennial,"* offered as the interpretive frame of the whole class. **[Stated, RV-1]** **[Analysis]** **Direct common ground with JD's own eschatology.** This is not a tension and should never be filed as one; it is one of the places where the two of them simply agree, and it is worth saying so out loud.
- **⭐ He rejects REACTIVE THEOLOGY by name, and states the principle positively (RV-14).** *"Many dispensationalists will deny this often due to an anti-Roman Catholic mindset where the impulse is to believe the opposite of what Rome believes,"* and then: *"We should do theology based upon a desire for the truth not as a reaction to a group we dislike. 2 + 2 = 4 regardless of who says it."* **[Stated, RV-14]** **[Analysis]** ⚠️ **The single clearest §15 item in the batch, and it should be credited plainly.** It is a methodological commitment JD shares, and **it is stated better than most Protestants state it.** It has a second use: it is **the standard he has set for himself**, available later as a *shared premise* rather than as a charge. ⚠️ **Do not deploy it as a gotcha. Log it as common ground and as his own stated standard.**
- **⭐ Councils RECOGNIZE truth, they do not CONSTITUTE it (RV-15).** *"councils to determine not to determine in the sense of like that they have the authority to say it's true or not true in making truth, right? But the power to recognize the Trinity, triune God. The power to recognize truths of the gospel, truths of the scriptures."* The self-correction mid-sentence is **his**, not ASR damage: he starts to say councils "determine," catches it, and rules the constitutive sense out. **[Stated, RV-15]** **[Analysis]** ⚠️ **Substantial common ground, and it is formulary-faithful.** The receptionist account of conciliar authority is the Anglican and the Reformed account both, and it is **inconsistent with a magisterial view**. **Do not treat as a lever.** It is also a datum for the Article VI two-tier thread: authority to *recognize* scriptural truth is not authority to *require* what Scripture does not prove (cf. DQ-12, RV-7). Cross-ref §3.
- **Word and sacrament as the ordinary Sunday expectation, in Article 28 compatible language (RV-9).** *"we gather together to receive both word and sacrament. The word of God and the body and blood of Christ."* **[Stated, RV-9]** **[Analysis]** "Receive the body and blood of Christ" is language **the Articles themselves use**. This is **common ground, not a lever.** It says nothing about sacrifice, and the Mass-as-sacrifice gap in the broader workstream is untouched by it. Cross-ref item 4 / `QA-Euc`.
- **Three incidental commitments worth crediting, grouped because none is a finding on its own (RV-23).** **[Stated, RV-23]**
  - **Hyper-preterism named a heresy and rejected:** *"There is a there's a heresy called hyper predatorism which believes that everything in revelation has already happened and we want to reject that too."* *(ASR: "hyper predatorism" for hyper-preterism.)*
  - **Simony refused, emphatically and unprompted:** *"We do not sell the sacraments. You will never have me selling the sacraments at all."*
  - **Scribal alteration of the text condemned,** on the 666 / 616 variant: *"which you shouldn't change the writings of scripture, but they did it."*
  - Add to these the extended defence of the **goodness of matter** against Gnosticism: *"We should never in our Christian faith look at the material world itself as evil,"* and *"The work of God in salvation includes the restoration of the universe itself."*
  - ⚠️ **All §15. None is a lever and none should be reworked into one.**

### RV-review common ground (added 260726-1, RV-vs-outline review)

*⚠️ **The §8 item 4 sweep was run against the RV review's outcomes and produced ONE item, not a batch.** That is the honest result and it is recorded as such. ### LS-series common ground (added 260728-1, batch 260727-2) — ⭐ the richest §15 harvest from any single batch

*⚠️ **Folded in during the SAME pass that logged the tensions**, per the §8 item 4 discipline. **Noted is not logged**, so they are here. ⚠️ **All of it is 2021-2022 and pre-St. Francis** — see the LS ledger's vintage warning. **A warm 2022 statement is evidence that he said it warmly in 2022.***

⭐ **This batch is unusually rich in unprompted, warmly stated common ground, and that is itself worth saying.** The three recordings are conversational rather than polemical, and **most of the creditable material below was volunteered, not extracted.** Five items, from a batch of twenty-two findings.

- **⭐ Baptismal regeneration is the formulary position, and Anglicans who deny it are evading their own standard (LS-4).** *"within the Anglican formulas ... we essentially hold to baptismal regeneration as well but people can and generally try to do play around with that trying to say we don't hold to that which we actually do."* **[Stated, LS-4]** **[Analysis]** ⛔ **Common ground, and the baptismal-regeneration lever is retired** (register, GV-38 `[→ item 9]`). Logged for balance and as a diagnostic datum. **Not a new lever, and this does not reopen one.** Held at `VP-3`, where the DELTA is **UNCHANGED**.

- **⭐ The written word itself conveys grace and is "a form of sacrament" (LS-5).** The Bible *"passes on Grace to us uh it is a form of Sacrament"*; *"scripture itself gives us the grace of God."* **[Stated, LS-5]** **[Analysis]** **An unprompted, warmly stated commitment to the sufficiency and efficacy of the read word, made AGAINST Rome and the East** — he faults both for sacramental focus at the expense of scripture reading, and faults much of Protestantism for the reverse. ⚠️ **This is a shared premise, not a charge**, and it is a notably good one to have in his own words in a project whose Bucket B is Reformed-versus-Anglican.

- **⭐ He denies that lacking apostolic succession unchurches anyone, and recommends Lutheranism to friends (LS-3, second half).** In the same passage in which he holds episcopal succession firmly, **he states twice that lacking it does not put one outside the church or under judgment.** **[Stated, LS-3]** **[Analysis]** ⚠️ **This is the warm half of a finding whose first half is a tension, and it must not be dropped when the first half is used.** It coheres with `LS-10`'s *plene esse* bounding and with the §1 datum that he has recommended Lutheranism and Eastern Orthodoxy to some (RC1-6). ⛔ **Not a lever; it is a limit he places on his own high-church commitment, and it should be credited as one.**

Explicit exceptions for excommunication and open defiance.

- **He has "a lot of respect for the Heidelberg" Catechism (LS-21).** *"I actually have a lot of respect for the Heidelberg. I I just like it."* **[Stated, LS-21 — ✅ verified RJ]** **[Analysis]** **Minor, and logged for balance rather than leverage.** Its use is register: **a warm, volunteered word for a Reformed confessional standard.** ⛔ **Not a lever** — he is agreeing to a historical custom, not subscribing anything.
